title: Lewis Spence, The Problem of Atlantis (1924; second edition 1925)

source.publisher: Internet Archive (user upload of the scan; Brentano's, New York, revised second edition, February 1925; first published May 1924)
source.license: Public domain (Lewis Spence died 3 March 1955, so UK copyright ended on 31 December 2025; published in 1924 and 1925, so US copyright has expired)

summary: A leading 1920s case for a real sunken Atlantic continent. It argues from geology, prehistory, myth and Central American and Egyptian archaeology; scholars do not accept the case. Useful for the history of the idea and for Spence's sources.

tool.name: hand-built (PageIndex format)
tool.method: Hand-built tree from the book's eighteen chapter headings (the contents page gives the printed page numbers, which are in the titles). Leaves are numbered in order; the text is the OCR of the upload with running heads removed, so OCR errors remain. No language model was used.

tree.title: Front matter: title page, prefaces and contents
tree.summary: Title page of the second edition (Brentano's, New York), the preface to the second edition, the contents and the list of plates.

tree.title: Ch. I (book pp. 1-10): The Atlantis of Plato
tree.summary: Spence introduces the persistence of the Atlantis legend and retells Plato's account of the island-continent sunk beneath the Atlantic.

tree.title: Ch. II (book pp. 11-32): Plato's account examined
tree.summary: A critical look at Plato's account, in which Spence argues that earlier writers dismissed it too lightly. He compares the plan of Carthage with the plan of the Atlantean capital.

tree.title: Ch. III (book pp. 33-45): The evidence from geology
tree.summary: An outline of geological time for non-scientific readers, followed by the geological evidence Spence offers for Atlantis, set in the Tertiary and the Ice Age.

tree.title: Ch. IV (book pp. 46-56): The biological evidence
tree.summary: Spence says he will use only the biological evidence he thinks fairly supports the Atlantis hypothesis, and admits that much of what is offered is of far less value.

tree.title: Ch. V (book pp. 57-72): The evidence from pre-history
tree.summary: Spence pictures Atlantis breaking up during the Ice Age and sending successive waves of people into Europe. He ties this to Plato's date of 9,000 years before Solon.

tree.title: Ch. VI (book pp. 73-82): The third Atlantean invasion
tree.summary: He takes the Azilian-Tardenoisian people, found in Spain and France about 10,000 years ago, as the next invasion after the Cro-Magnons, and follows their remains.

tree.title: Ch. VII (book pp. 83-91): The evidence from European tradition
tree.summary: European legends of lands that once lay in the Atlantic. Spence says others have collected them and gives a selection.

tree.title: Ch. VIII (book pp. 92-102): The evidence from American tradition
tree.summary: Spence argues that if western Europe remembered the break-up of an Atlantic continent, American tribes would have echoed it, and turns to their traditions of cataclysm.

tree.title: Ch. IX (book pp. 103-114): The evidence from American tradition, continued
tree.summary: Continues with American tradition, starting from Mexican water gods such as Tlaloc, whose festivals he reads as memories of a deluge.

tree.title: Ch. X (book pp. 115-119): The Popol Vuh as an Atlantean record
tree.summary: Spence recalls his early doubts about the American origin of the Popol Vuh and argues that it holds traditions of an Atlantean past.

tree.title: Ch. XI (book pp. 120-139): The evidence from Central American archaeology
tree.summary: He takes Maya culture as the best picture of civilisation in "Antilia", the last sub-continental fragment of Atlantis, and describes the architecture and art that he says link Central America with the Old World.

tree.title: Ch. XII (book pp. 140-148): The evidence from Central American archaeology, continued
tree.summary: Continues with Maya sculpture and painting, such as the two-headed dragon at Copan, read as figures connected with cataclysm or the sea.

tree.title: Ch. XIII (book pp. 149-162): The evidence from Egypt
tree.summary: Spence takes up the debated theory that Egyptian civilisation had an Atlantean origin and confines himself to evidence that he says links Egypt with the Atlantic world.

tree.title: Ch. XIV (book pp. 163-181): Egyptian and American comparisons in the light of Atlantean research
tree.summary: He sets out the resemblances between Egyptian and American civilisations, citing the school of Professor G. Elliot Smith, and says they spring from one source.

tree.title: Ch. XV (book pp. 182-196): The evidence from old Peru
tree.summary: Spence describes the architectural remains scattered over the western slope of the Peruvian Andes, among the most remarkable produced by the aboriginal American race, and their place in his argument.

tree.title: Ch. XVI (book pp. 197-210): The geography and topography of Atlantis
tree.summary: Spence argues that the plan of the Atlantean capital was copied far and wide, and reconstructs the geography and topography of Atlantis.

tree.title: Ch. XVII (book pp. 211-226): The Flood
tree.summary: Spence reviews the main flood accounts, Biblical and pagan, and asks whether they preserve a memory of the cataclysm that destroyed Atlantis.

tree.title: Ch. XVIII (book pp. 227-232): Conclusion
tree.summary: Spence attempts to reconstruct life in Atlantis, admits that enthusiasm has at times outrun caution, and ends by calling the work the beginning of a quest for the bones of Atlantis.
